name: PT Bank Jago Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank Jago: a real franchise that does not yet earn its cost of equity
frontmatter.summary: Bank Jago has a genuine digital franchise, a large customer base and a cheap deposit mix, but it does not earn its cost of equity and the price assumes it soon will. Write-offs already exceed the non-performing ratio and the cost ratio has stopped falling. On the stock's own measured risk we cut to REDUCE with a target of Rp430.
thesis: The franchise is real but the return is not: loans and deposits still grow at a high-teens rate and more than half of deposits are CASA, yet return on equity stays below the cost of equity for most of the forecast [S2].
The discount to book is not a margin of safety: the shares trade at 0.8x book, but at the cost of equity built from the stock's own regression beta the justified multiple is lower still [S14].
Credit is the swing factor: the charge is held at the observed run-rate and write-offs exceed the gross NPL ratio, so the sub-one-percent NPL is not the buffer it looks like [S15][S2].

Cost has stopped falling: the ratio improved through 2025 but personnel and other expenses still rose in the first nine months of 2026, so the long-run target is far shallower than the previous note assumed [S9][S2].
The fee pool is not yet a profit stream and the register is concentrated, so there is no second engine to justify a premium to book [S2][S5].

catalysts.event: Close of the employee share option exercise window
Monthly banking credit and deposit release from the regulator
First policy meeting of the year and the rate decision
Full-year results and the first guidance for the coming year

blocks.text: We cut Bank Jago to REDUCE with a target of Rp430, a total return of -16.5% from a share price of Rp515 [S0]. The stock has fallen from a year high of Rp2,220 to a low of Rp496 and now changes hands at 0.8x our forward book value [S0][S14]. A deep discount to book is usually where a bank re-rating starts; here it is where the arithmetic ends.

Our target is built from two methods that price the same return path: justified P/BV at Rp445 and residual income at Rp311, blended and rolled forward one year at a cost of equity of 15.3% [S14][S15]. Both methods use a sustainable return on equity of 11.7%, which is below the cost of equity. The franchise does not earn excess returns even at maturity, and the two methods differ by -30.3% because residual income charges the early years of shortfall that the P/BV formula ignores. We weight residual income at 65% for that reason.

The cost of equity is the load-bearing input, so we set it out in full in section four. It is built from the house macro deck: the ten-year IDR sovereign yield of 7.4% less the sovereign default spread of 1.6%, plus beta times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5%, plus a small-capitalisation premium of 0.6%. The beta is 1.33, the stock's own three-year weekly regression against the Jakarta Composite Index, not the industry default. That combination gives 15.3%, which is above the house ERP band for IDR names; we argue the exception below and show the in-band alternative in the sensitivity table, where the value sits close to the current price.

The variant view is therefore narrow and specific. We agree with the market that the franchise is real and that the loan book will keep growing; we disagree with the cost of equity the price implies. At the top of the house band for IDR names the current price is close to fair, as section four shows; the stock's own measured volatility says the required return is higher than the band assumes, and at that rate a bank that only reaches its cost of capital at the end of a decade is worth less than its book.

What moves the value. First, the credit charge: it is the largest single drag on the return path and the item with the widest range of outcomes [S15]. Second, the cost ratio: a technology-heavy cost base spread over a growing loan book is the mechanism that lifts return on equity from 4.5% to 11.6%, and the first nine months of 2026 show the decline has stalled [S2]. Third, the cost of equity itself: a one-point change moves the target by roughly the width of the rating band, which is why we publish the grid rather than a point estimate.

Because the bank has never paid a dividend and we model none, the dividend discount model returns nothing by construction and carries no weight; the whole value sits in the two methods that capitalise the return on equity path [S4][S0]. The principal risks are a partner-channel credit shock, a funding squeeze, a rights issue that dilutes per-share value, and the concentration of the register [S16][S5].

Bank Jago is an Indonesian commercial bank that runs a digital-only model: it takes deposits and lends through a mobile application rather than a branch network, and it serves retail customers, mass-market savers and small businesses with both conventional and syariah products [S5]. The bank began life as Bank Artos and was acquired and repositioned as a digital lender in 2019 by Jerry Ng and Patrick Walujo, whose vehicles remain the controlling shareholders [S5].

The product set has broadened from a savings app into a full balance sheet. On the funding side the app offers savings and time deposits, a foreign-currency pocket and a digital card aimed at individual business users, while the syariah version serves customers who want a Sharia-compliant account [S12]. On the lending side the bank lends through ecosystem partners, digital platforms and multifinance companies including BFI Finance, and it has begun to lend directly to app users through Jago Dana Cepat [S12][S10].

The customer base is the operating engine, and the series needs care. The bank served 19.0 million customers at the end of September 2026, of whom 13.1 million were funding customers [S2]. Two quarters earlier it reported 20.1 million customers and 14.7 million funding customers [S18][S19], and at the end of FY2025 it reported 18.2 million and 14.2 million [S12]. So both series rose through the first half and then fell in the third quarter. The company defines the funding series as active savings customers who use the Jago app [S19][S18], and deposits still grew at a double-digit rate over the same period [S2]; we therefore read the third-quarter step-down as a restatement or a purge of inactive accounts rather than a collapse in the deposit franchise. It is a line we will watch, but it is not a thesis-breaker on its own. Deposits were IDR28,855.6bn at the end of September, of which current and savings accounts were 53.0% [S2]. More than half of the deposit base is therefore cheap transactional money, which is unusual for a challenger bank and is the main reason its cost of funds is competitive [S2].

Net interest income is the overwhelming majority of revenue: IDR2,300.0bn in the first nine months of 2026, against fee and commission income of IDR13.3bn [S2]. Other operating income was IDR419.3bn in the same period, so non-interest revenue is dominated by treasury and partner income rather than card or account fees, and it tracks the size of the balance sheet more than the number of customers [S2]. That matters for the valuation: the fee pool that a mature retail bank relies on has barely started to form, and we do not capitalise one.

Management's plan is to keep growing through the ecosystem partners while building direct lending, and to spend on technology and data rather than on branches [S12]. The 2026 business plan contains no inorganic growth: management said at the public expose that no merger or acquisition is contemplated, including the BFI Finance combination that had been speculated about in the press [S6]. Growth is therefore organic, and the capital position is the constraint on how fast it can be funded [S6][S2]. The company has publicly linked investment in artificial intelligence to operating efficiency, which is consistent with the cost path we model [S6].

Strategically the bank is a challenger, not an incumbent. Its loan book of IDR27,875.6bn is a small fraction of the 9,245 trillion rupiah of credit in the banking system [S2][S16], and its 596 employees administer a balance sheet that a branch network would need many times the headcount to run [S0]. The addressable market is therefore not the constraint; underwriting and funding are.

Indonesian banking is unusually concentrated, and the large incumbent banks enjoy a funding advantage built on decades of deposit relationships and a branch presence that reaches into small towns. A digital bank does not compete on branch convenience; it competes on price, on the speed of opening an account, and on being embedded in an app that the customer already uses every day. Digital banks in Indonesia are licensed and supervised on the same capital, liquidity and asset-quality rules as incumbents, so their advantage is a low marginal cost per account rather than a regulatory subsidy. A digital bank with a small loan book carries a large fixed technology cost relative to revenue until the book scales, which is why cost-to-income ratios at challengers start high and fall as the balance sheet grows. The model is inherently front-loaded in cost and back-loaded in profit.

The operating environment is supportive but slowing. System bank credit reached Rp9,245tn in September 2026 and grew 13.3% year on year, down from 13.7% in August [S16]. The composition matters for a bank like Jago: investment credit grew 23.2% and corporate borrowers led by category, while lending to micro, small and medium enterprises grew only 2.7% [S16]. The growth is coming from large-ticket corporate and investment lending, not from the consumer and small-business segments where a digital bank competes.

Deposits grew more slowly than loans. Third-party funds rose 8.2% to Rp10,492tn in the same month, so the system loan-to-deposit ratio is rising and deposit competition is the binding constraint on loan growth [S16]. For a challenger that funds itself mostly from retail balances rather than corporate relationships, that is both an opportunity, because savers shop for yield and convenience, and a risk, because deposit pricing is set by the largest banks and a small bank has to pay up to attract balances [S16].

The policy rate was held at 5.75% at the October meeting, but the corridor was not unchanged: the deposit facility was raised to 5.00% and the lending facility was held at 6.50% [S17]. A higher deposit facility is a direct cost for a bank that holds central-bank balances and a signal that the floor under deposit competition has moved up. The central bank framed the decision around contained inflation and rupiah stability [S17]. With real GDP growth of 5.3% as the backdrop, the economy is not the problem; the absence of rate cuts is. A flat policy rate removes the easing tailwind that flattered margins in the previous phase, so any margin expansion has to come from mix rather than from the curve [S17][S2].

Competition comes from three directions: incumbent banks moving onto apps, other digital banks, and non-bank lenders and multifinance companies that already own the customer relationship [S10]. Jago's answer is to be the balance sheet behind other people's customers: it lends through ecosystem platforms and multifinance partners rather than acquiring every borrower itself [S12][S10]. That keeps customer-acquisition cost low and lets the bank scale a book faster than its brand would allow, but it concentrates credit risk in a small number of partners and leaves the bank with less pricing power on the asset side [S10].

The moat is thin. Switching costs for a savings customer are close to zero, the app is easy to copy, and the partner relationships are contracts rather than ownership [S10]. What the bank does have is a low cost base, a full banking licence, a deposit franchise that has reached critical mass, and a shareholder group with deep banking experience [S5][S9]. We treat those as advantages that protect the return on equity path, not as a franchise that can earn excess returns indefinitely [S9].

On the five-forces reading, buyer power is high because depositors and borrowers can switch at no cost, supplier power is low because technology is bought in the market, the threat of new entrants is high but the licence and capital requirements slow it, and rivalry is intense because the large banks are defending share with digital products of their own [S16][S10]. Substitutes, chiefly multifinance and fintech lending, are the strongest force: they compete for exactly the consumer credit Jago wants to write, and they have the customer relationship first [S10]. Regulation is a constant rather than an event: capital, liquidity and asset-quality rules are the same as for incumbents, and the bank reports a capital ratio well above the minimum [S2]. On our arithmetic the bank holds a fraction of one percent of system credit, so share gains are available without taking them from any single competitor [S16].

Indonesian credit is intermediated mostly by a handful of large banks and a long tail of small ones, with multifinance companies and, more recently, digital lenders serving borrowers who sit outside the formal payroll and collateral base. A challenger bank grows by taking share from multifinance and by lending to people the incumbents have not underwritten, which means its credit losses are a function of a customer segment with no long track record through a downturn. The segment's losses are low in good years and can step up quickly when unemployment rises or when a partner changes its underwriting, which is why the market applies a discount to fast-growing consumer lenders even when reported asset quality looks clean.

The history is a growth story with a thin profit base. Loans rose from IDR17,701.5bn in FY2024 to IDR24,346.6bn in FY2025, and deposits from IDR18,916.2bn to IDR26,031.3bn, both up by close to two fifths [S14][S12]. Net interest income rose from IDR1,553.4bn to IDR2,466.0bn, and net profit more than doubled, from IDR128.5bn to IDR276.2bn [S15][S12]. Total assets reached IDR36,507.3bn, so the balance sheet roughly doubled in two years while profit remained a small fraction of equity [S14].

The first nine months of 2026 kept the pace. Net profit was IDR298.1bn, up by half year on year, on net interest income of IDR2,300.0bn [S2]. The impairment charge rose to IDR883.1bn from a much lower base, and operating costs rose too, so the profit growth came from revenue outgrowing a heavier cost and credit line rather than from a one-off gain [S2]. Loans reached IDR27,875.6bn and deposits IDR28,855.6bn at the end of September, and total assets reached IDR42,102.1bn [S2][S14].

The profit and loss has to be read on two bases, and the difference matters. On the reported statements the FY2025 bridge closes exactly: net interest income of IDR2,466.0bn plus non-interest income of IDR438.5bn, less operating expenses of IDR1,700.4bn and a provision charge of IDR853.0bn, gives pre-tax profit of IDR351.1bn [S15]. The data pack carries lower revenue lines because it classifies part of each elsewhere: its net interest income is IDR2,340.6bn and its non-interest income is IDR225.1bn, and the engine's history therefore shows an "other items" plug of IDR338.7bn that restores the reported pre-tax profit [S15][S14]. That plug is a data-pack artefact, not an income stream: it is the gap between the pack's revenue lines and the reported revenue lines, and carrying it into the forecast would double count. The forecast is built on the reported definition, with non-interest income rebased to the reported level, so the FY2026E bridge closes on operating lines without a plug.

The other operating income inside that line is recurring, not a one-off. It was IDR438.2bn for the whole of FY2025 and IDR419.3bn in the first nine months of 2026, against fees of IDR13.3bn [S15][S2]. So it is mostly treasury and partner income that scales with the balance sheet, and it is already inside the non-interest income base the forecast grows; we do not add it twice, and we do not assume it disappears.

Margins are high by Indonesian standards and gently declining. On the reported statements the net interest margin was 7.2% in FY2025, and the nine months of 2026 ran at about the FY2026E level we carry, so the forecast starts at the observed run-rate rather than stepping up from the data pack's lower line [S15][S2]. We then let the margin slip five basis points a year: the policy rate is flat, time deposits are just under half of funding and reprice with the corridor, and lending yields face more competition as other digital banks scale [S2][S17]. With the deposit facility raised to 5.00%, the deposit-beta assumption matters: we assume roughly half of the time-deposit book reprices with the corridor and almost none of the CASA book, which is why the corridor change costs a few basis points of margin rather than more [S17][S2].

Cost is where the operating leverage has stalled. The cost-to-income ratio fell from 74.0% to 59.0% in the nine months to September 2025, and management said it expects it to keep falling [S9]. But the 2026 accounts do not continue that trend: personnel expense rose to IDR465.9bn and other expenses to IDR961.1bn in the first nine months, both up year on year, and the reported ratio for the period was about the FY2026E level we carry rather than below it [S2]. We therefore hold the ratio at 52.0% for FY2026E and let it decline to 47.0% by the end of the horizon, a much shallower path than the previous note assumed. The decline is built from the cost lines: technology, marketing and other expenses grow at roughly half the rate of the loan book once the platform is built, while personnel grows with the customer base. The first nine months of 2026 show other expenses growing faster than revenue, so the near-term direction is up, not down; the long-run decline is an operating-leverage assumption, not an extrapolation of the recent trend [S2][S9].

Credit is the earnings-quality flag, not the growth. The gross NPL ratio rose from 0.6% to 0.9%, still far below the system average [S12][S2]. The provision charge is much larger than the NPL ratio implies: 4.1% of average loans in FY2025, and the first nine months of 2026 annualise to the 4.5% we carry for the full year [S15][S2]. We hold that run-rate rather than stepping it down: the nine-month charge of IDR883.1bn was up from a much lower base a year earlier, and a lower full-year number would require a fourth-quarter step-down the company has not guided to [S2].

The provisioning-versus-write-off trend is the flag the earnings-quality screen is designed to catch, and it is adverse. In FY2025 the provision charge was IDR853.0bn while the allowance rose only from IDR288.7bn to IDR552.5bn, so most of the charge left the balance sheet as write-offs rather than staying in reserves [S15][S14]. In the first nine months of 2026 the charge was IDR883.1bn against a further build from IDR552.5bn to IDR763.2bn, and the same pattern holds [S2][S14]. On average loans that implies write-offs running at a multiple of the 0.9% gross NPL ratio: the NPL ratio is being managed down by writing off bad loans, not only by recovering them or by classifying them. The archived sources do not carry special-mention, restructured-loan or stage-three balances, and the annual report is not in the archive, so we cannot say how much of the book sits in the watchlist categories; that is a gap in the evidence, and it is why the long-run charge is held above the NPL ratio rather than converged to it [S15][S14][S2].

Capital is ample but falling, and the dilution question is real even if it is not immediate. The capital adequacy ratio went from 31.6% at FY2025 to 27.5% at September 2026 as lending grew into the buffer, and our model has it easing to 19.8% by the end of the horizon [S12][S2]. That is still well above the regulatory floor, so a rights issue is not required to keep the bank compliant. But the payout basis is right that the book consumes capital faster than it earns it: at high-teens loan growth and a risk density of 1.2x, the buffer falls by roughly a few points of capital a year, and any acceleration or credit shock would bring a raise forward. We model no raise in the base case because none is announced, but the bear case contains one (section five), and the per-share impact is the reason the bear is worth less than the base.

Our forecast compounds loans to IDR98,310.8bn by FY2035E, takes net profit to IDR2,496.9bn, and lifts return on equity from 4.5% to 11.6% [S14][S2]. That endpoint is deliberately unheroic: it is below the cost of equity we use, and on our cost of equity it produces a value below the current price. The loan-to-deposit ratio is held near 95.1% rather than allowed to creep toward the ceiling, and the mix stays close to today's, with no fee-led transformation assumed [S2].

A bank is valued on its equity, not on enterprise cash flow, so the method set is justified P/BV, residual income and, in principle, a dividend discount model [S14]. Justified P/BV prices the spread between sustainable return on equity and the cost of equity; residual income does the same thing year by year and adds a terminal value; the dividend model only works when the bank pays out [S15]. For a bank with no dividend, the first two are the only ones that carry information.

The cost of equity is the denominator of both methods and of the roll-forward, so we set out the build in full rather than leaving it to the model. The risk-free rate is the house macro deck's ten-year IDR sovereign yield of 7.4%; the engine subtracts the sovereign default spread of 1.6% to reach a local risk-free rate, then adds beta times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5%, and a small-capitalisation premium of 0.6%. Debt is set to zero because a bank's liabilities are its funding rather than leverage in the discounted-cash-flow sense, so the cost of capital equals the cost of equity [S14].

The beta is the input that changed. The previous note used the BANKS industry default, which is just under one, because the universe beta file carried no regression for the stock; that default is recorded exactly in the assumptions file and in the industry configuration. We now carry a company parameter from the house regression: three years of weekly returns against the Jakarta Composite Index to the start of November 2026 give a raw beta of about one and a half, a Blume-adjusted beta of 1.33 and an R-squared of about a third; the one- and two-year windows give similar estimates, so the result is stable. The weekly return series and the regression output are not in the evidence archive, so the beta is disclosed as a company parameter and an evidence gap rather than a figure a reader can rebuild from the archived sources. It is consistent with a stock that fell from Rp2,220 to Rp496 over the year and whose drawdown is far larger than the index's [S0].

The small-capitalisation premium of 0.6% is the remaining judgement. It covers the stock's size (a market capitalisation of IDR7,138.6bn), its free float of 27.2% and a three-month average daily turnover of IDR15.5bn [S0]. That is a genuinely small, thinly traded line for an institutional buyer, and a premium at the lower end of the small-cap range is appropriate; we have not changed it from the previous note.

The resulting cost of equity of 15.3% is above the house ERP band for IDR names, which is a deliberate exception and needs to be argued. The band is a prior for a mature, liquid Indonesian financial; it is not a cap. ARTO is neither mature nor liquid, its own regression beta is well above the sector default, and at the top of the band the cost of equity would be lower and the value would sit close to the current price. We disclose both because the rating is sensitive to the choice: the sensitivity table below shows the target against the cost of equity and terminal growth, and the value falls as the cost of equity rises. A reader who prefers the band's top should read the target as roughly fairly valued rather than as a sale; a reader who accepts the regression should read the current price as too high for the risk. We take the regression because it is the stock's own measured risk, and because the industry default for a name with this volatility is not a conservative assumption but an unexamined one.

On a sustainable return on equity of 11.7% and terminal growth of 4.0%, the justified multiple is 0.7x book, or Rp445 per share on our FY2026E book value of Rp664 [S14]. That multiple looks low in absolute terms, and it is: the franchise does not earn its cost of capital even at maturity, so it is worth less than the equity on its balance sheet. The question the market is answering is only whether it is worth a little less or a lot less.

Residual income gives Rp311, -30.3% versus justified P/BV [S15]. The divergence is the point, not a problem to be averaged away. Justified P/BV capitalises a mature return on equity on today's book, which flatters a franchise whose return is below the cost of equity for most of the forecast; residual income charges that shortfall year by year and then capitalises what is left. The residual-income answer is the more conservative and the more internally consistent, so we weight it at 65% and treat P/BV as the cross-check it is meant to be. The two methods also use slightly different book bases, the P/BV formula on forward book value and residual income on the opening equity at the balance-sheet date; that is a second reason not to give the P/BV answer the larger weight.

The dividend discount model carries no weight. The bank pays no dividend and we can find no distribution in any year of the price history, the annual meeting that approved the FY2025 accounts declared none, and we model a zero payout because the loan book needs the capital [S4][S0]. A model that discounts zero dividends returns zero by construction, so including it would inject a number that says nothing about the business; we moved its weight to the two methods that price the return path.

The fee pool is not in the numbers, and that is a deliberate omission rather than an oversight. Fee and commission income was IDR13.3bn in the first nine months of 2026, a small fraction of non-interest income [S2]. Even a modest fee take on the deposit base would be material to profit at near-full margin, and the customer base is the distribution channel for it. We exclude it because the bank has not demonstrated an attach rate, the 2026 accounts show fees growing but from a very low base, and capitalising a stream that does not yet exist would be the kind of optimism the accounts do not support. What would change that: two or three quarters of fee income growing faster than deposits, a disclosed attach rate on a named product, or a fee-to-deposit ratio disclosed by management. Until then the fee pool is an option, not a value.

What the price implies for the franchise is worth stating plainly. The market pays IDR7,138.6bn for IDR9,138.8bn of equity, a licensed bank with 19.0 million customers, a CASA share of 53.0% and IDR28,855.6bn of deposits [S14][S2]. On our numbers the market is not assigning negative value to the licence or the customer base; it is paying less than book because the return on that equity is below the cost of capital and the book is growing faster than the profit that supports it. A strategic buyer would face the same arithmetic: the licence and the deposit base are worth something, but the buyer would also inherit a sub-cost-of-capital return path and a partner-channel credit book that has not been through a downturn. That is why a control premium is a possibility, not a floor, and why we do not value the franchise option separately.

Blending the two methods at their weights gives a value of Rp358 today; rolled forward one year at the cost of equity and without a dividend to deduct, that is Rp413 in the base case [S14]. Probability-weighting the scenarios gives Rp430, which is our target of Rp430, an expected return of -16.5% from Rp515 [S0].

As a cross-check the shares trade on 17.7x our FY2026E earnings and 0.8x book [S14]. A bank that earns a return below its cost of equity should trade below book; the question is how far below. Our 0.7x answer implies that the current 0.8x is too high, not that the bank deserves a premium to book.

The first risk is credit. The partner-channel book has grown faster than the bank's own underwriting experience, the NPL ratio is still below one percent, and the charge is several times the NPL [S2][S15]. A partner that underwrites worse than expected, or a consumer segment that seasons badly in a slowing economy, would hit both the charge and the growth rate at once. Because the bank lends through partners, it sees the loss after the partner has seen the borrower, which shortens its reaction time.

The second is funding. The loan-to-deposit ratio is 96.6% and deposits grew more slowly than loans in the system [S2][S16]. The deposit facility was raised to 5.00% at the October meeting, which raises the floor under deposit competition [S17]. If deposit competition intensifies, either the margin falls or growth slows; our bear case assumes both, with a lower margin and loan growth three points below the base case [S16].

The third is capital and dilution. The base case has no rights issue because none is announced and the capital ratio stays well above the regulatory floor. But the book consumes capital faster than it earns it, and a credit shock or an acceleration in growth would bring a raise forward. The bear case therefore includes one: growth only three points below the base case, the capital ratio falling toward the floor, and a rights issue priced at a discount to book. We model the dilution as an increase in the share count of two points a year, which is a proxy for one or two discounted raises over the horizon, and it lowers per-share value in the bear by roughly the dilution rate. That is the risk the previous note removed by cutting growth in the bear; we now model it explicitly.

The fourth is competition and regulation. Incumbent banks are building the same products, multifinance already owns the customer, and the regulator can change capital or provisioning rules [S16][S10]. None of these is a base-case event, but together they cap how far the multiple can re-rate. A higher risk weight on unsecured consumer lending would also slow the capital release that funds growth [S2].

The fifth is the register. A controlling shareholder group holds most of the equity, the free float is 27.2%, and the shares trade IDR15.5bn a day, so a large seller would move the price [S5][S0]. The option programme adds a small amount of dilution, and the absence of a dividend means the return depends entirely on the multiple [S7][S4]. Liquidity risk and governance risk are the same risk here: a concentrated register is a two-way price.

Our scenarios are mirrored around the base case. In the bear case the credit charge is eighty basis points above the base case, the margin is forty basis points lower, loan growth is three points slower and the share count grows two points a year for a discounted rights issue, and the value falls to Rp285 at a 25.0% weight. In the bull case the same four shocks run in reverse: the charge is eighty basis points lower, the margin forty basis points wider, growth three points faster and the share count two points lower as surplus capital is returned, and the value rises to Rp610 at 25.0% [S12][S9]. The base case carries 50.0% and a value of Rp413. The spread is wide because the value is dominated by the terminal spread between return on equity and the cost of equity, and that spread is small and sensitive to both inputs.

What would change our view: a charge that falls durably without new NPL formation, evidence that the cost ratio is falling again in the 2026 accounts, a fee stream that grows faster than deposits and is disclosed, or a strategic transaction at a premium to book. On the downside, a partner failure, a funding squeeze that forces a higher deposit rate, a rights issue at a deep discount, or an IDX notation or board change would each justify a lower value. The signposts are quarterly and public, which is why we are comfortable holding the rating through the next print.

Control sits with two vehicles. PT Metamorfosis Ekosistem Indonesia holds 29.8% and Wealth Track Technology Limited holds 11.7%, and the two act as controlling shareholders; Metamorfosis is the vehicle of Jerry Ng, a career banker, and Wealth Track is associated with Patrick Walujo [S5]. Insiders hold 72.5% in total, institutions 9.9%, and the free float is 27.2% [S0]. The register has been stable since the original acquisition, with no evidence of pledged-share selling in the disclosures we have archived [S5].

The annual meeting in May 2026 approved the FY2025 accounts and appointed a new director, Nicholas Tan, for the 2026-2029 term, alongside the existing chief executive and compliance director [S4]. There is no dividend and no buyback, and none is proposed [S4]. The board is therefore asking shareholders to fund growth entirely through retained earnings, which is consistent with the capital path in the model but leaves the return dependent on the multiple [S4][S2].

The employee option programme is the only known issuance: up to 38.5 million shares at Rp1,550 exercisable between November and December 2026, which is a small fraction of the shares outstanding [S7]. At a strike well above the current price the options are out of the money, so the dilution is more likely to be a signal about retention than about capital, and the cash raised is immaterial [S7].

Governance is typical of a founder-controlled Indonesian bank: a concentrated register, a founder in the chair, and a board recently refreshed [S5][S4]. The mitigant is that the controlling shareholders are career bankers with reputational capital at stake, and the bank has raised equity rather than extracted it [S5][S4]. We would treat a related-party transaction with an ecosystem partner, or a change in the controlling stake, as a governance event that requires a fresh look at the discount.

The related-party and partner-channel exposure cannot be quantified from the archive. The annual report, which would carry the related-party note and the partner-concentration disclosure, is not in the archive: the company's investor site refuses automated access. We have searched the company releases, the nine-month and half-year results, the MESOP announcement and the public-expose coverage, and none of them breaks out loans by partner or related party [S2][S6][S7][S18][S19]. What we can say is that the two controlling vehicles hold 29.8% and 11.7% [S5], that the lending model is built on named partners including BFI Finance [S10], and that the absence of a partner-concentration disclosure is itself a governance limitation. A reader should treat the partner concentration as an unquantified risk rather than a measured one.

On the IDX regime checks, we found no special-monitoring board status and no special notation in the archive, despite the drawdown: the stock is in the regular market with a free float above the minimum and a liquid enough tape for the strategy [S0]. That is not a clean bill of health on the accounts, which are unaudited at the quarterly stage; it is the absence of the regime flags that would gate investability. We will re-check the board and notation status at each results date.

The ESG profile is dominated by data and inclusion rather than emissions. A digital bank's material issues are customer data protection, cybersecurity and responsible lending, and its positive contribution is financial inclusion for customers the branch network does not reach [S5]. The credit-risk flag in the previous section is also the social-risk flag: fast consumer lending to a thin-file segment is exactly where conduct and over-indebtedness risk sits [S10]. We see no evidence of a governance or environmental issue that would change the valuation, but we flag the data and conduct exposure as the area where a problem would be most damaging to the franchise.

The nearest dated event is the close of the option exercise window in December 2026, which settles the dilution question for the year [S7]. The FY2026 results in the first quarter of 2027 are the first full-year test of the cost and credit path, and the monthly regulator release gives an early read on system credit and deposit growth in between [S16]. The central bank's rate meetings matter less directly, because the policy rate is expected to stay where it is, but a move in either direction would change the deposit pricing assumption [S17].

The KPIs we monitor are loan and deposit growth, the loan-to-deposit ratio, the cost-to-income ratio, the credit charge against the NPL ratio, the CASA share, the capital ratio and, now, the funding-customer count [S2][S9]. Each is disclosed quarterly, and the combination tells us whether the return on equity path in the model is being delivered or whether the bank is buying growth with margin and credit [S12]. We also watch the fee line and any partner-concentration disclosure, because either would change the valuation more than another quarter of loan growth.

A re-rating needs one of three things: evidence that the charge is a growth cost rather than a loss, evidence that the cost ratio can fall further without stalling growth, or evidence that the fee pool is becoming a real stream. Any of them would lift the sustainable return on equity and with it the justified multiple. None is in the price today, and the price already assumes a cost of equity below the one the stock's own volatility implies. We would revisit the rating on a material divergence between the reported charge and the NPL trend, a capital action that changes the share count by more than the option programme, or a sustained fall in the cost of equity as the stock's liquidity and volatility improve [S7][S2].

bear.narrative: The partner-channel book seasons badly: the credit charge runs eighty basis points above the base case (roughly 5.3% in FY2026E, above the observed nine-month run-rate) and the allowance keeps building, NIM is forty basis points lower as deposit competition bites, loan growth is three points below the base case as partners pull back, and the capital shortfall against a 15% CAR target is closed with a rights issue at a discount to book that adds two points a year to the share count. ROE never closes the gap to COE and the stock stays a sub-book value story.

bull.narrative: The direct-lending build (Jago Dana Cepat) and the ecosystem partners scale: the credit charge is eighty basis points below the base case as the low NPL holds and the allowance build stops, NIM is forty basis points wider as CASA grows, loan growth is three points faster, and surplus capital above the regulatory floor is returned rather than raised, which reduces the share count by two points a year. ROE reaches the mid-teens by the end of the decade.

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E reproduces the run-rate: gross loans reached Rp27.9tn at Sep-2026, +19% yoy (S2), and a normal Q4 takes the year to about Rp29tn, i.e. +19% on the FY2025 Rp24.3tn (S14). Growth then decelerates two points a year as the base grows: the FY2025 rate of 38% (S12) halved to 19% in nine months (S2), and the partner-channel model (ecosystem platforms, multifinance partners such as BFI Finance, S10) cannot keep compounding at 2025's rate off a book that has doubled. The 13% long-run rate is set at a modest premium to nominal GDP (5.3% real plus ~3% inflation, macro deck) for a franchise that is still taking share.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: Deposits of Rp28.9tn at Sep-2026 were +21% yoy (S2) and Rp26.0tn at FY2025 (+38%, S14/S12), so FY2026E of +17% lands near Rp30.5tn. Funding keeps pace with the loan book rather than outgrowing it: LDR was 96.6% at Sep-2026 (S2) and 94% at FY2025 (S12), leaving almost no headroom, so the deposit path runs a point behind loan growth in FY2026 and then in line with it, holding LDR near 95% through the horizon rather than letting it creep toward the regulatory ceiling, and the CASA mix (53% of deposits, S2) is assumed stable because the digital wallet is the funding engine.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: Total assets / gross loans was 1.50x at FY2025 (Rp36.5tn / Rp24.3tn, S14). Total assets is the earning-asset base used here (F9/F10); the ratio drifts down slowly as lending outgrows the liquidity portfolio (cash and securities), reaching 1.45x by FY2030. It never falls below 1.4x because a 96%+ LDR bank still holds central-bank cash and government securities against deposits.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: Measured on the reported statements, NIM was 7.57% in FY2025 (reported NII Rp2,466bn, F14, over average total assets of Rp32,505bn, F7/F8) and 7.80% for the nine months to Sep-2026 (NII Rp2,300bn annualised, F22, over average assets of Rp39,305bn). FY2026E of 7.75% is therefore the observed run-rate, not a step up: the 7.20% that the engine's history line shows is the data pack understating NII by Rp125bn (pack Rp2,341bn against reported Rp2,466bn, F14/S15), an artefact corrected in the FY2026E base. The base case then lets the margin slip five basis points a year: the BI rate is flat at 5.75% with the deposit facility raised to 5.00% (S17), so there is no tailwind, time deposits are 47% of funding and reprice with the corridor (S2/S18), and the lending yield is set by partner and consumer products that face more competition as the digital banks scale. Deposit beta is assumed near 0.5 on the time-deposit half and near zero on CASA, which is why the 25bp deposit-facility increase costs roughly 5bp of NIM rather than more.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: The FY2026E step is a BASE CORRECTION, not growth. The data pack carries FY2025 non-interest income of Rp225bn, but the reported statement shows Rp438bn (F16) and the nine months of 2026 alone produced Rp433bn (other operating income Rp419bn plus fees Rp13bn, S2). The pack omits the same other operating income line on both sides of the ledger, so the level is restored to the reported run-rate (Rp225bn x 2.19 = Rp493bn, about the twelve months to Sep-2026) and grown 13%/12%/11%/10% after that. The long-run 9% is the fee pool: fee and commission income was only Rp13.3bn in nine months (S2), so most of this line is treasury and partner income that tracks the balance sheet rather than the customer count.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: FY2026E holds the observed nine-month ratio, not a forecast of further gains. Reported FY2025 cost-to-income was 58.5% (opex Rp1,700bn, F18, over reported total operating income of Rp2,904bn = NII Rp2,466bn, F14, plus NOII Rp438bn, F16); the 9M-2026 ratio was 52.2% (opex Rp1,427bn over TOI Rp2,733bn, S2). The 55% previously carried was 2.8pp above the 9M26 observation and is withdrawn. The drift from 52% to 47% long run is 5 points, not the 9 points previously assumed, and is built from the cost lines rather than a trend: personnel rose 14% yoy to Rp466bn and other expenses rose 30% to Rp961bn in 9M26 (S2), so the near-term driver is technology and marketing spend growing with the customer base; the decline comes from those lines growing at roughly half the rate of the loan book (15-19% a year) once the platform is built. The 9M26 cost lines contradict a faster decline, which is why the path stops at 47%.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: FY2026E holds the observed nine-month run-rate rather than stepping it down. The 9M-2026 charge was Rp883.1bn on average gross loans of Rp26,111bn (F21, F2/F3), i.e. 4.51% annualised, so 4.5% for the full year implies a Q4 charge in line with the Rp294bn quarterly run-rate instead of the Rp210bn a 4.1% year would have required. The 9M26 charge was itself up from Rp623.1bn in 9M25 (S2), so the trend is still rising, not normalising; we do not assume a Q4 step-down without a company allowance target to support it. The path then normalises the growth-driven allowance build out as loan growth slows, to 2.9% long run - above the 0.9% gross NPL (F25) and above the FY2024 charge (F19), because the partner channel has not been through a full downturn and, as the provisioning-versus-write-off trend in the report shows, write-offs are already running well above the NPL ratio.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: No non-operating line is carried in the forecast, but the history's Rp338.7bn line is not a non-operating item and must not be read as one. On the reported statements the FY2025 bridge closes exactly: NII Rp2,466bn (F14) + NOII Rp438bn (F16) - opex Rp1,700bn (F18) - provisions Rp853bn (F20) = pre-tax Rp351.1bn (F?/S15). The engine's history plug of Rp338.7bn is the data pack's understatement of the same two revenue lines (pack NII Rp2,341bn and NOII Rp225bn against reported Rp2,466bn and Rp438bn, F14/F16/S15); it is a data-pack artefact, not an other-income stream, and carrying it forward would double count. The forecast NOII base is the reported level (Rp438bn grown to Rp493bn, see noii_growth), which already contains the other operating income that made up Rp419bn of the Rp433bn nine-month 2026 non-interest total (S2), so the forecast is on the reported definition. The report publishes both bridges so a reader can see the two bases.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The statutory 22% rate under UU HPP (macro deck, tax_rate_id) against an FY2025 effective rate of 21.3% (tax Rp74.9bn on pre-tax Rp351.1bn, S15). No permanent timing differences are large enough to justify anything else.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Bank Jago is a single consolidated entity with no minority interests in the data pack or in the reported statements (minority Rp0 in every year, S0/S14).

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: ARTO has never paid a dividend: no distribution appears in any year of the price history (S0, dps_ttm 0) and the RUPST that approved the FY2025 accounts declared none (S4). With loans growing 15-19% a year and RWA density of about 1.17x loans, retained profit is the growth capital: at a 15% CAR target the loan book needs roughly Rp600bn of new capital a year against FY2026E net profit near Rp400bn, so a payout would force another rights issue. We therefore model zero payout through the horizon.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: The only known issuance is the MESOP tranche: up to 38.53m shares at Rp1,550 exercisable between 2 November and 11 December 2026 (F42/F43, S7), i.e. 0.28% of the 13,861m shares outstanding (S0). No rights issue is planned.

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: Implied from the reported capital ratio: equity Rp8,826bn / CAR 31.6% gives RWA of Rp27,930bn against gross loans of Rp24,347bn at FY2025 (1.147x); equity Rp9,139bn / CAR 27.5% gives RWA of Rp33,232bn against Rp27,876bn of loans at Sep-2026 (1.192x). The mean of the two, 1.17x, is used and held flat; a shift toward unsecured consumer lending would push it up, which the bear case captures through slower capital release rather than a separate shock.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: Terminal growth is 4%, the house default for an IDR reporter, and it is deliberately below the nominal GDP anchor rather than derived from it. The macro deck has real GDP growth of 5.3% and CPI of 3.28%, so the nominal anchor is about 8.6%; the previous basis wrongly described 4% as "real growth less an inflation differential". We use 4% because the terminal value is applied to residual income, not to revenue: a franchise that does not earn its cost of equity should not be assumed to compound at the economy's nominal rate in perpetuity, and capitalising an 8.6% growth rate on a sub-COE spread would inflate the negative franchise value. The choice is NOT immaterial: the PV of the terminal value is about minus Rp1,537bn, roughly 36% of the residual-income equity value, and the published sensitivity grid moves the target by about Rp16-27 per point of g, about Rp73 between 4% and the 8.6% nominal anchor. The direction is also the opposite of the one previously stated: because residual income is negative on this path, a LOWER g raises the target (3% gives about Rp427 against Rp413 at 4% and Rp395 at 5%), so 4% is less conservative, not more, than the nominal anchor. It is retained as the house default and because a sub-COE franchise should not be held to nominal GDP growth in perpetuity, not because the choice is small or safe.

challenges.challenge: The model's FY2025 history carries other_nonop of Rp338.7bn (FY2024 Rp283.2bn), 13% of total operating income, and sets it to zero from FY2026E. The basis says "the FY2025 profit bridge closes exactly on NII + NOII - opex - provisions ... so there is no residual to model". On the engine's own lines the bridge is 2,340.6 + 225.1 - 1,700.4 - 853.0 + 338.7 = 351.1, so a Rp338.7bn residual exists and is dropped. History and forecast are therefore on different revenue definitions, and no audited LK or auditor opinion is in the archive to settle which is right.
challenges.answer: The challenge is right and the previous basis was wrong. The Rp338.7bn line is the data pack's understatement of NII (pack Rp2,340.6bn vs reported Rp2,466.0bn) plus NOII (pack Rp225.1bn vs reported Rp438.5bn); the reported bridge closes exactly and the pack bridge needs the plug. The line is recurring, not a one-off: other operating income was Rp419.3bn of the Rp432.6bn nine-month non-interest total, and it is already inside the NOII base the forecast grows. Both bridges are now published in section three, the basis is rewritten, and the forecast is stated to be on the reported definition. The audited LK is not in the archive, so the restatement rests on the reported statements (S15) and the nine-month release (S2); that limitation is disclosed.

challenges.challenge: credit_cost FY2026E of 4.1% is described as "the observed level", but the 9M26 charge of Rp883.1bn annualises to ~4.5% of average loans (Rp26.1tn). FY2026E of 4.1% implies Q4 provisions of ~Rp210bn against a Rp294bn quarterly run-rate, a 29% step-down in the quarter with no source. This is the largest single value driver by the report's own account.
challenges.answer: Held at the observed run-rate. FY2026E credit cost is now 4.5%, which is the 9M26 charge of Rp883.1bn annualised over average gross loans of Rp26,111bn (4.51%), and the path then normalises to 2.9% long run. The unsourced Q4 step-down is withdrawn; the basis states that a 4.1% year would have required a Q4 charge of about Rp210bn against the Rp294bn quarterly run-rate, and that the 9M26 charge was itself up from Rp623.1bn a year earlier. The value impact is in the model and the sensitivity table.

challenges.challenge: The write-off rate is never computed. Gross charge Rp853.0bn less the allowance build of Rp263.8bn implies ~Rp589bn written off, 2.8% of average loans and 3.1x the 0.9% gross NPL. The report reads the same gap as prudential provisioning ("we assume the former") without any special-mention, restructured or stage-3 data. EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS requires the provisioning-versus-write-off trend for a financial, and it is absent.
challenges.answer: The trend is now computed and disclosed as adverse. FY2025: charge Rp853.0bn, allowance up Rp263.8bn (F64 to F11), so the balance leaves as write-offs rather than reserves. 9M26: charge Rp883.1bn against a build from F11 to F12, the same pattern. On average loans that is a write-off rate at a multiple of the 0.9% gross NPL, so the NPL is being managed down by write-offs. Section three now says exactly that, and the long-run charge is held above the NPL rather than converged to it. The SML, restructured and stage-three balances are NOT in any archived source and the annual report is not obtainable, so the table is limited to charge, allowance build and the implied write-off; that gap is stated as an evidence limitation rather than papered over.

challenges.challenge: Funding customers fell from 14.2m to 13.1m (-7.7%) while total customers rose to 19.0m, and the report dismisses it as "either a change in how the company counts ... or a sign that new accounts are less engaged" with no source. Deposits +21% on 7.7% fewer funding customers means deposits per funding customer rose ~31%: either a definitional break or depositor concentration. Separately, S17 shows the deposit facility was raised to 5.00%, not merely held, while 47% of deposits are time deposits and the model lets NIM fall only 5bp a year.
challenges.answer: Sourced. The series is 18.2m/14.2m at FY2025 (S12), 20.1m/14.7m at 1H26 (S18, S19) and 19.0m/13.1m at 9M26 (S2). The company defines funding customers as active savings users of the Jago app (S19, S18), and both series rose then fell together in Q3, so the step-down is a restatement or purge of inactive accounts rather than a franchise collapse; deposits still grew 21% over the period. Section one now carries the full sourced series. On the corridor, section two now states that the deposit facility was RAISED to 5.00%, and the NIM basis carries an explicit deposit beta of about 0.5 on the 47% time-deposit book and near zero on CASA, which is why the 25bp step costs roughly 5bp of NIM.

challenges.challenge: COE 12.45% is the denominator of both methods and of the roll-forward, but the build is never disclosed: rf 7.45%, an effective ERP of ~4.9% (at or below the house 5.0-6.0% IDR band), an unexplained 60bp premium, and an unlevered beta of 0.9 taken as a default because "no 3y weekly regression exists" - for a stock that fell from Rp2,220 to Rp496. The engine's own grid puts the 12-month value near Rp568 with COE 1pp higher and ~Rp480 at 2pp higher, i.e. the Rp515 price is the model's value at a ~14% COE.
challenges.answer: The COE build is now fully disclosed in section four: rf is the house ten-year IDR sovereign yield (7.45%), less the sovereign default spread (1.62%), plus beta x (ERP 4.23% + CRP 2.46%), plus a 0.60% small-cap premium. The regression was run: three years of weekly returns to the JCI, 154 observations to 2 November 2026, raw beta 1.49, Blume-adjusted 1.33, R-squared 0.31; the 2y and 1y windows give 1.33 and 1.24. Beta is now 1.33, which lifts COE to 15.33% - above the house band. That exception is argued explicitly in the report, which also states that at the top of the band the value is near the current price. The COE sensitivity grid is in the report as {{table:sensitivity}}, not only in the model.

challenges.challenge: Justified P/BV, at 55% weight, applies the FY2035 sustainable ROE of 11.65% to a FY2026E book of Rp659 (0.905x) while the model's own ROE is 4.5% in FY2026, 6.2% in FY2027 and 8.1% in FY2028. Capitalising a decade-out ROE on today's book is the method's known overstatement; the residual-income method on the same path produces Rp561, and the report does not explain the Rp36 gap.
challenges.answer: Accepted in the weights and in the prose, not in the formula (the engine's justified-P/BV method applies the mature ROE to forward BVPS and is not parameterised to fade). The treatment is now: residual income, which charges the early shortfall year by year, carries 65%; justified P/BV, which capitalises a decade-out ROE on today's book, is demoted to a 35% cross-check. Section four states that the P/BV method overstates value for a franchise below its cost of equity for most of the path, explains the divergence as the early-year shortfall that RI charges and P/BV ignores, and also notes the differing book bases (forward BVPS vs the 30 Sep equity). The blended value, and therefore the target, moves accordingly.

challenges.challenge: Capital. CAR fell from 31.6% to 27.5% in nine months; at 19% loan growth and 1.17x RWA density, RWA grows ~Rp5.9tn in FY2026E against Rp404bn of retained earnings, so the buffer is consumed at ~4.4pp of CAR a year. The payout basis itself says the book "needs roughly Rp600bn of new capital a year against FY2026E net profit near Rp400bn" - a recurring shortfall - yet no rights issue or dilution is modelled in any scenario, and "no rights issue is planned" rests on a MESOP article (S7). The bear cuts loan growth 3pp, which removes the dilution risk instead of modelling it.
challenges.answer: The bear case now models the dilution instead of cutting growth around it. It adds 2 points a year to the share count as a proxy for one or two discounted rights issues over the horizon, holds the credit shock and the margin squeeze, and produces a lower per-share value; the bull case mirrors it with a 2-point reduction for capital return above the regulatory floor, so the shocks remain symmetric for the QC gate. Section three now says explicitly that the buffer falls a few points of CAR a year at high-teens growth and that any acceleration or credit shock would bring a raise forward, and section five describes the capital-raise risk in full. Base case still assumes none because none is announced.

challenges.challenge: The fee pool is valued at nothing. Fees were Rp13.3bn in nine months, 4% of non-interest income; non-interest income is grown 9% long-run and no retail fee stream is modelled. Even 25bp of fees on Rp30tn of deposits is ~Rp75bn, ~19% of FY2026E net profit at near-100% margin, and the 19.0m customers are the distribution channel for it.
challenges.answer: Accepted as a disclosure, not as a number. Section four now states the fee pool explicitly: fee and commission income was Rp13.3bn in nine months, a small fraction of non-interest income; the pool is excluded because the bank has disclosed no attach rate and the accounts show fees growing only from a very low base; capitalising a stream that does not yet exist would be unsupported. The report names what would change the treatment (two or three quarters of fee growth ahead of deposits, a disclosed attach rate, or a fee-to-deposit ratio) and adds the fee line to the monitoring KPIs. No peer fee-to-deposit ratio is used because that would require peer data outside the archive; the scenario is left as an option rather than a valuation input.

challenges.challenge: The market pays Rp7,139bn for Rp9,139bn of equity - a licensed bank with 19.0m customers, a 53% CASA franchise and Rp5.7tn of cash - so the franchise, licence and deposit base are assigned negative value. The report notes 0.78x book but never values the franchise or the strategic/control option. The BFI combination was press-speculated; S6 records only that management has no plan, which is not the same as no possibility.
challenges.answer: Added. Section four now states what the price implies: the market pays Rp7,138.6bn for Rp9,138.8bn of equity, a licensed bank with 19.0m customers, a 53% CASA share and Rp28.9tn of deposits (S14, S2). It explains that the market is not assigning negative value to the licence; it is paying below book because the return on equity is below the cost of capital. It also explains why a strategic buyer would face the same arithmetic - the licence and deposit base are worth something, but the buyer inherits a sub-COE return path and a partner-channel book that has not been through a downturn - so a control premium is a possibility, not a floor, and we do not value the franchise option separately. No replacement-cost estimate is given because no sourced cost per deposit customer exists in the archive.

challenges.challenge: CTI FY2026E of 55.0% is described as "the observed level", but the 9M26 actual is 52.2% (opex Rp1,427bn over TOI Rp2,733bn). The first forecast year is ~2.8pp conservative, ~Rp100bn of opex, ~3% of FY2026E net profit, and the basis note misstates the observed data.
challenges.answer: FY2026E is now 52.0%, the observed nine-month ratio (opex Rp1,427bn over total operating income Rp2,733bn), not 55%. The 55% was 2.8pp above the observation with no source and is withdrawn. The basis now shows the two ratios explicitly - FY2025 58.5% on the reported definition and 9M26 52.2% - and the forecast path runs 52/51/50/49/48 to a 47% long run.

challenges.challenge: The 46% long-run CIR is a 9pp drift whose only source (S9, 1 Nov 2025) describes 9M25. The 9M26 accounts show other expenses up 30% yoy to Rp961bn and personnel up 14% to Rp466bn, so the CIR decline had stopped before the forecast begins. The QC gate is answered with a trend that the most recent data contradicts.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The long-run target is cut from 46% to 47%, a 5-point drift rather than 9, and the path is now built from the 9M26 cost lines: personnel Rp465.9bn (+14% yoy) and other expenses Rp961.1bn (+30% yoy), with the decline coming from those lines growing at roughly half the 15-19% loan-growth rate once the platform is built. conservatism_audit.note: Two directions. Conservative: FY2026E CTI 55% against 52.2% observed (C10); terminal g 4% against a ~8.6% nominal anchor; zero payout forever with no terminal distribution even though ROE sits below COE. Optimistic: credit cost 4.1% against a 4.5% run-rate (C2); NIM 7.20% to 7.75% (+55bp) in FY2026E with a flat BI rate and 47% time deposits; no dilution despite a recurring capital shortfall (C7).
